structure.title: **Just Accepted**
structure.text:
"Just Accepted" manuscripts have been peer-reviewed and accepted for publication. They are posted online prior to technical editing, formatting for publication and author proofing. The American Chemical Society provides "Just Accepted" as a free service to the research community to expedite the dissemination of scientific material as soon as possible after acceptance. "Just Accepted" manuscripts appear in full in PDF format accompanied by an HTML abstract. "Just Accepted" manuscripts have been fully peer reviewed, but should not be considered the official version of record. They are accessible to all readers and citable by the Digital Object Identifier (DOI®). "Just Accepted" is an optional service offered to authors. Therefore, the "Just Accepted" Web site may not include all articles that will be published in the journal. After a manuscript is technically edited and formatted, it will be removed from the "Just Accepted" Web site and published as an ASAP article. Note that technical editing may introduce minor changes to the manuscript text and/or graphics which could affect content, and all legal disclaimers and ethical guidelines that apply to the journal pertain. ACS cannot be held responsible for errors or consequences arising from the use of information contained in these "Just Accepted" manuscripts.

structure.title: Correlation of structure and fast ion conductivity in the solid solution series $\text{Li}_{1+2x}\text{Zn}_{1-x}\text{PS}_{4}$
structure.text:
Kavish Kaup, a Fabien Lalère, a Ashfia Huq, b Abhinandan Shyamsunder, a Torben Adermann, c Pascal Hartmann, c and Linda F. Nazara\* - a Department of Chemistry, Department of Chemical Engineering and the Waterloo Institute for Nanotechnology, University of Waterloo, 200 University Ave W, Waterloo, Ontario N2L 3G1, Canada - b Neutron Scattering Division, Oak Ridge National Laboratory - c BASF SE, Ludwigshafen, Germany **ABSTRACT:** Solid electrolytes are the foundation of all-solid-state batteries (ASSB) and have the potential to provide improved safety and higher energy density than existing liquid battery systems. In the important search for new lithium ion conductors with fast ionic conductivity and good mechanical properties, thiophosphates are a particularly promising class of materials. The first experimental elucidation of new lithium ion conductors in the $Li_{1+2x}Zn_{1-x}PS_4$ (LZPS) solid solution whose existence had been predicted by theory is reported herein. Using neutron and synchrotron x-ray powder diffraction together with electrical impedance, and Raman studies, we resolve their crystalline nature and correlate this with ionic conductivity upon increasing the lithium/zinc ratio. We demonstrate that the materials exhibit high experimental ionic conductivities - up to $8 \times 10^{-4}$ S·cm-1 - and show the nature of likely pathways for lithium ion conduction. Rechargeable all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) using inorganic solid electrolytes (SE) have become one of the most promising alternatives to conventional Li-ion batteries that use flammable organic liquid electrolytes. Inorganic SEs have the potential to enable batteries that are not only safer but have higher energy density, low temperature performance and longer cycle life1-3. To realize the potential of ASSBs, new SE materials are sought that can adequately replace the current liquid electrolytes. These materials require fast lithium ion conduction (>10-4 S·cm-1), a wide electrochemical stability window, and chemical compatibility with both the anode and cathode4-8. While a range of various lithium-ion conductors exist and have been studied9, sulfides show the most promise in terms of ionic conductivity and processability4,8. Sulfides are very ductile, making them easily processed via cold-pressing. Notable sulfide type lithium-ion conductors that exhibit some of the highest ionic conductivities comparable to liquid electrolytes stem from the lithium thiophosphate family. These include the argyrodites, 10 Li10GeP2S12 (LGPS: 12 mS·cm-1)11 and its Si/Sn derivatives12-14, Li7P3S11 (17 mS·cm-1)15,16, and most recently LGPS-type $\text{Li}_{9.54}\text{Si}_{1.74}\text{P}_{1.44}\text{S}_{11.7}\text{Cl}_{0.3}$ (25 mS·cm-1)17 which exhibits the highest room temperature lithium ion conductivity to date. Recently, Richards et al. 18 used density functional theory and *ab initio* molecular dynamics to investigate the Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 (LZPS) system, which exhibits a bodycentered cubic (bcc) sulfur sublattice. Theory suggests that this arrangement of sulfur atoms, which is also adopted by two other fast ion conductors (Li7P3S11 and LGPS), is correlated to a low lithium migration barrier. 19 The stoichiometric parent phase LiZnPS4 and its optical properties have been previously reported but no ionic conductivity data was provided. 20,21 Its structure consists of a frame-ACS Paragon Plus on the 2d site. work of $PS_4^{3-}$ and $ZnS_4^{6-}$ tetrahedra that house Li+ ions, where Li fully occupies the 2b site and Zn fully occupies the 2a site (**Figure 1a**). In the Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 nonstoichiometric phases (**Figure 1b**) the additional Li shares the 2a site with Zn as we show below, with the excess Li distributing equally between the 2a and an additional site, 2d. This 2d site is close to the "interstitial" site that was not explicitly identified in the theoretical work.17 The stoichiometric phase was predicted to have extremely poor conductivity based on first-principles calculations (1.81 x $10^{-12}$ S·cm-1, Ea = 1.07 eV), while the introduction of interstitial lithium defects is predicted to yield ionic conductivities greater than $5 \times 10^{-2}$ S·cm-1 (with Ea > 0.17 eV) at room temperature up to a solid solution solubility limit of x = 0.5; 18 i.e., Li2.0Zn0.5PS4. Here, we report the synthesis of the solid solution series, and the structure of the member within the solubility limit with the highest predicted conductivity, derived from combined X-ray and neutron powder diffraction analysis. ![](_page_1_Figure_13.jpeg) **Figure 1.** a) Crystal structure of stoichiometric LiZnPS4; b) non-stoichiometric, showing addition of interstitial Li in the 2a site shared between Li and Zn and partial occupancy of Li for the Advistor. The highest value of x (i.e. of lithium excess) in a well crystallized sample was x = 0.35, corresponding to Li1.7Zn0.65PS4. We unequivocally identify lithium occupation of the 2d site, which is charge compensated by substitution of a Zn2+ ion in the 2a site with Li+ and is crucial for improving ionic transport. Experimental ionic conductivities (σi) measured by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) show that the σiof the most highly conductive phases are in the range of > 10-4 S·cm-1 at 25˚C: a very significant improvement over LiZnPS4, albeit less than predicted. Phases with high values of x (> 0.5) were experimentally unattainable as relatively pure crystalline phases, however. Our observations demonstrate that the enhancement in ionic conductivity observed in the x = 0.75 phase is likely due to a glass-ceramic matrix effect rather than from its inherent crystalline structure. Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 compositions were prepared at x = 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75 using solid-state synthesis consisting of ballmilling and annealing. Their synchrotron x-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns are shown in **Figure 2**. The compositions contain small impurities of Li4P2S6 and ZnS which form upon slight decomposition of the LZPS solid solutions because of their metastable nature. As the lithium content increases (up to x = 0.75), the formation of significant γ-Li3PS4 impurities becomes evident, in accord with the pseudo-binary phase diagram calculated by Richards *et al.*18 . ![](_page_2_Figure_5.jpeg) **Figure 2.** Synchrotron powder X-ray diffraction patterns (25°C) of Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 (x = 0.25), Li2Zn0.5PS4 (x = 0.5), and Li2.5Zn0.75PS4 (x = 0.75) with impurities of Li4P2S6, ZnS, and Li3PS4 as marked. Region with the dashed box is expanded on the right, indicating the shift in the (112) reflection (4 space group) towards higher angle. The corresponding synthesis temperatures are listed above the compositions. The *a* and *c* lattice parameters were extracted by performing a Pawley full powder pattern fit of the synchrotron XRD patterns in the 4 space group. The trends are shown in **Figure 3** (with exact values given in **Table S1**), indicating that the cell volume increases with increased lithium content (293 Å3 to 301 Å3). The increase in cell volume stems from a significant increase in the *a* lattice parameter (with a small decrease in the *c* lattice parameter). Larger lattice volume often correlates to an improvement in ionic conductivity due to a reduced Li+ ion migration barrier. 19, 22 Since the targeted Li2Zn0.5PS4 phase is expected to have the highest ionic conductivity within the solid solution solubility limit, its crystal structure was refined against combined synchrotron powder X-ray diffraction data (λ = 0.412 Å) and time-of-flight (TOF) neutron diffraction data. ![](_page_2_Figure_8.jpeg) **Figure 3.** Lattice parameter and volume change in Li1+2xZn1 xPS4 for x = 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75. Solid black circles are from single crystal data taken from the literature19 and blue squares are experimental data from this work (values are listed in **Table S1**). The reflections were assigned to a body-centered tetragonal cell (space group 4, no. 82) with lattice parameters refined to *a* = 5.7945(2) Å, and *c* = 8.8337(3) Å. The crystallographic details are summarized in **Table 1a** (we note that bond lengths, **Table S2**, are typical for all environments) while the fit for the synchrotron and neutron data is shown in **Figure 4**. The results of the refinement indicate that the actual lithium content of the crystalline material is x ≈ 0.35; lower than that targeted (i.e. x = 0.5). The crystalline ![](_page_2_Figure_12.jpeg) **Figure 4.** Combined Rietveld refinement of "Li2.0Zn0.5PS4" based on synchrotron x-ray diffraction and neutron diffraction data. Visual representation of the refined crystal structure (refined to a composition of Li1.7Zn0.65PS4) is shown as an inset. Excluded regions correspond to impurity phases, mainly Li4P2S6 which comprises < 5% of the total (see **Figure 2**). **Table 1a.** Atomic coordinates, Wyckoff symbols, and isotropic displacement parameters for the targeted Li2Zn0.5PS4 phase in the space group 4 (no. 82). the space group 14 (no. 82). | Atom | Wyck.

The degree of crystallinity was estimated to be 69% using Si as an internal reference (**Figure S1**). A proposed mixture of [77% Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 + 23% *a*-Li3PS4] accounts for the overall "Li2.0Zn0.5PS4" target. The 8% discrepancy may be attributed to the impurity phases (Fig. 2). The refined structure of Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 shows that the 2a sites are partially occupied by Li (34%) and Zn (66%) while the 2d site has partial occupancy of Li (34%) as visually represented in the inset in **Figure 4**. Owing to the well-known difficulty in simultaneously refining thermal parameters and occupancies, the thermal parameters for the 2d and 2b site were fixed to average values from the literature.11,17,23,24 This resulted in convergence to site occupancies that yielded perfect charge balance of the compound and an equal distribution of excess Li on the 2d and 2a sites as expected. The results are in excellent accord with *ab initio* molecular dynamics studies that predict significant lithium ion density on an "interstitial site",17 which is similar to the 2d Wyckoff site we identify. While Li2.5Zn0.25PS4 (x = 0.75) was projected by theory to have the highest conductivity (1.14 x 10-1 S·cm-1),17 its structure could not be refined owing to the low quality of the X-ray and neutron data for this poorly crystallized compound. This is in accord with it lying just out of the predicted solubility limit.17 The structure of "Li1.5Zn0.75PS4" was refined from the synchrotron X-ray data owing to its low lithium content (and a paucity of neutron time); and these results are shown in **Table 1b.** The fit is shown in **Figure 5;** refined bond lengths (**Table S2**) correspond to typical values for all environments. The lattice ![](_page_3_Figure_8.jpeg) **Figure 5.** Rietveld refinement of "Li1.5Zn0.75PS4" synchrotron x-ray diffraction data only. Excluded regions correspond to impurity phases, mainly Li4P2S6, which comprises <10% of the total (see **Figure 2**). **Table 1b.** Atomic coordinates, Wyckoff symbols, and isotropic displacement parameters for the targeted Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 phase in the space group 4 (no. 82) | Atom | Wyck.

Since lithium can not be accurately refined from X-ray data, lithium occupation in the 2d and 2a site was fixed to be equal, as determined by the Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 formulation. The Zn occupancy was refined and the vacant occupancy was assumed to be lithium given that the 2a site occupancy is constrained to 1*.* The refined composition of Li1.2Zn0.9PS4 (with a 70% degree of crystallinity determined by standard addition) shows that the target composition was also not achieved in this case. This may be due to slow kinetics of the reaction that prevent achievement of the targeted lithium contents, despite the employment of nano-sized ZnS in the synthesis (see Supporting Information). However, synthesis at higher temperature or longer times is limited by thermodynamics: due to the metastability of the substoichiometric phases, the LZPS structure partially decomposes to Li4P2S6. The formation of such impurity phases can be prevented by heating at lower temperatures; however, this comes at the cost of reduced degree of crystallinity. The importance of excess phonon free energy in stabilizing defect-type ionic conductors with highly mobile Li+ ion lattices has been previously invoked, for example, in Li7P3S11, and especially in Li1+2xZn1-xPS4.17 We note that the limiting composition Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 (x = 0.35) is approximately halfway between the predicted solubility limit for the solid solution series without phonon contributions (x = 0.15) and with phonon contributions (x = 0.5)18. Clearly Li1.2Zn0.9PS4 (x = 0.1) falls within in the regime where phonon contributions are not necessary to stabilize the material. All experimental attempts to increase the degree of lithium substitution to attain x = 0.5 were unsuccessful irrespective of temperature, time and processing conditions - and resulted in significant levels of impurity phases. These results confirm that phonon contributions do play a vital role in stabilizing these defect structures but likely to a lower degree than presumed. Partial occupancy of Li in the 2a and 2d site in the LZPS structure should facilitate the ion conduction by creating low energy percolating pathways through the structure. The Li+ ion conductivity of the various LZPS compositions was studied using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) on pressed pellets at variable temperatures. The impedance spectra in Nyquist form showed classic semicircles at high frequency, and a linear Warburg component in the low-frequency range (**Figure 6a)**. Fitting the data (see inset for equivalent circuit and **Table S3** for fit parameters) resulted in experimental conductivities at 25°C plotted in **Figure 6b** as a function of lithium content. ![](_page_4_Figure_3.jpeg) **Figure 6.** a) Activation energy plot of Li2Zn0.5PS4 and Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 along with an inset of the Nyquist plots at each temperature plus the equivalent circuit used to fit the impedance data and b) Li+ ion conductivity at 25˚C versus x in Li1+2xZn1-xPS4**.** Predicted values are taken from ref. 18. The conductivities range from 5.40 × 10-8 S·cm-1 at x = 0 to 8.4 × 10-4 S·cm-1 at x = 0.75. The conductivity of the refined phase Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 was 1.30×10-4 S·cm-1, which is lower than predicted for either Li2.0Zn0.5PS4 (5.38 x 10-2 S·cm-1) or Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 (2.77 x 10-2 S·cm-1) as shown in **Figure 6**. The amorphous content may be responsible, although temperature-dependent conductivity measurements exhibit Arrhenius behavior with a low activation energy of 0.22 eV. This value is close to the range predicted by MD simulations for the defect phases,18 namely 0.165 eV (Li2.0Zn0.5PS4) and 0.181 eV (Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 ). While the possible amorphous phase (i.e., *a*-Li3PS4; σi = 2.8×10-4 S·cm-1 ) 25 may contribute to the overall conductivity, its much lower reported activation energy of 0.4 eV suggests that the σi of Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 dominates. Similarly, the refined phase Li1.2Zn0.9PS4 has a room temperature ionic conductivity of 1.65×10-5 S·cm-1, which is lower than the predicted Li1.25Zn0.875PS4 phase (3.44×10-3 S·cm-1), but the activation energy is 0.25 eV, quite close to theory (0.252 eV18). The highest ionic conductivity of 8.4 x 10-4 S·cm-1 was achieved when the x = 0.75 glassy precursor was heated at lower temperatures (230˚C) to form a very poorly crystallized material. An SEM image of its featureless morphology is shown in **Figure S2**. Heating above that temperature results in a lower ionic conductivity of 2.4 x 10-4 S·cm-1 , and clear phase separation of the LZPS solid solution and γ-Li3PS4. The high conductivity in the glassy phase formed at low temperature is exclusive to the x = 0.75 compound (**Table S3**). Postulating that the improvement in ionic conductivity arises from the glass-ceramic nature of the material, we probed the local structure of Li2.5Zn0.25PS4 via Raman spectroscopy, and compared it to the other two phases. (**Figure S3**). While Li2.0Zn0.5PS4 and Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 show predominantly PS4 3- moieties characteristic of the crystalline structure (along with Li4P2S6 impurity), the more highly conductive Li2.5Zn0.25PS4 synthesized at low-temperature contains an additional peak in the Raman spectrum not present in the other two compositions. It corresponds to P2S7 4- units; inherent building blocks in the crystalline fast lithium ion conductor Li7P3S11. 16 They exist in its amorphous precursor (70:30 Li2S-P2S5 glass), which is known to have very high conductivities of >10-4 S·cm-1 before annealing 25. This leads us to propose that the glassy matrix plays a significant role in the high ionic conductivity of "Li2.5Zn0.25PS4", rather than inherently enhanced pathways in the structure. In summary, our results provide an understanding of ion transport in the Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 solid solution series by defining the complex relationship between lithium site occupation/position and ionic conductivity. *Ab initio* computational techniques provide inspiration and guidance in the search for new solid-state ion conductors. Here, we have compared the results of introducing interstitial lithium defects in in the solid solution regime Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 predicted by theory, with that of experiment. The stability of the defect phases owing to phonon contributions may be somewhat overestimated by theory, as all phases are found to be highly metastable. Such metastability results in difficulty in overcoming the kinetics necessary for mass transport in order to access the pure phases at the low temperatures required for their synthesis. Nonetheless, phases close to the targeted Li2.0Zn0.5PS4 and Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 were successfully synthesized. Their structures were elucidated via refinement of diffraction data. The obtained phases, Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 and Li1.2Zn0.9PS4 respectively, demonstrated ionic conductivities of 1.30×10-4 S·cm-1 and 1.65×10-5 S·cm-1. These values are more than four orders of magnitude higher compared to that of the parent LiZnPS4 phase, owing to occupation of the 2d interstitial site in the lattice as predicted by theory. This represents a good demonstration of how information from *ab initio* molecular dynamics can augment experiment, similar to Li10GeP2S12, where early reports using powder diffraction alone could not locate a lithium site important to 3D mobility, but a combination of theory and single crystal diffraction enabled full structure resolution.11,26–28 While our experimental lithium ion conductivities were lower than predicted, this can be ascribed to a combination of not fully accessing the targeted lithium defect concentrations (owing to the limitations of kinetics and thermodynamics), and the accompanying reality of the presence of amorphous and potentially poorly conductive materials. The fact that we can synthesize solid solutions close to the predicted superionic phases is encouraging, however, and suggests that alternate highly non-equilibrium synthetic routes may be required to access pure phases. This should provide further inspiration for future endeavors. Moreover, LZPS compositions at high lithium contents – Li2.5Zn0.25PS4 - exhibit conductivities up to 8 x 10-4 S·cm-1, showing that a glassy matrix can play a key role in governing fast lithium ion conduction.

nodes.title: Authors and Abstract
nodes.text:
Kavish Kaup, <sup>a</sup> Fabien Lalère, <sup>a</sup> Ashfia Huq, <sup>b</sup> Abhinandan Shyamsunder, <sup>a</sup> Torben Adermann, <sup>c</sup> Pascal Hartmann, <sup>c</sup> and Linda F. Nazar<sup>a</sup>\*

- <sup>a</sup> Department of Chemistry, Department of Chemical Engineering and the Waterloo Institute for Nanotechnology, University of Waterloo, 200 University Ave W, Waterloo, Ontario N2L 3G1, Canada
- <sup>b</sup> Neutron Scattering Division, Oak Ridge National Laboratory
- <sup>c</sup> BASF SE, Ludwigshafen, Germany

**ABSTRACT:** Solid electrolytes are the foundation of all-solid-state batteries (ASSB) and have the potential to provide improved safety and higher energy density than existing liquid battery systems. In the important search for new lithium ion conductors with fast ionic conductivity and good mechanical properties, thiophosphates are a particularly promising class of materials. The first experimental elucidation of new lithium ion conductors in the  $Li_{1+2x}Zn_{1-x}PS_4$  (LZPS) solid solution whose existence had been predicted by theory is reported herein. Using neutron and synchrotron x-ray powder diffraction together with electrical impedance, and Raman studies, we resolve their crystalline nature and correlate this with ionic conductivity upon increasing the lithium/zinc ratio. We demonstrate that the materials exhibit high experimental ionic conductivities - up to  $8 \times 10^{-4}$  S·cm<sup>-1</sup> - and show the nature of likely pathways for lithium ion conduction.

nodes.title: Introduction to All-Solid-State Batteries and Sulfide Electrolytes
nodes.text: Rechargeable all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) using inorganic solid electrolytes (SE) have become one of the most promising alternatives to conventional Li-ion batteries that use flammable organic liquid electrolytes. Inorganic SEs have the potential to enable batteries that are not only safer but have higher energy density, low temperature performance and longer cycle life<sup>1-3</sup>. To realize the potential of ASSBs, new SE materials are sought that can adequately replace the current liquid electrolytes. These materials require fast lithium ion conduction (>10-4 S·cm-1), a wide electrochemical stability window, and chemical compatibility with both the anode and cathode<sup>4-8</sup>. While a range of various lithium-ion conductors exist and have been studied<sup>9</sup>, sulfides show the most promise in terms of ionic conductivity and processability<sup>4,8</sup>. Sulfides are very ductile, making them easily processed via cold-pressing. Notable sulfide type lithium-ion conductors that exhibit some of the highest ionic conductivities comparable to liquid electrolytes stem from the lithium thiophosphate family. These include the argyrodites, <sup>10</sup> Li<sub>10</sub>GeP<sub>2</sub>S<sub>12</sub> (LGPS: 12 mS·cm<sup>-1</sup>)<sup>11</sup> and its Si/Sn derivatives<sup>12-14</sup>, Li<sub>7</sub>P<sub>3</sub>S<sub>11</sub> (17 mS·cm<sup>-1</sup>)<sup>15,16</sup>, and most recently LGPS-type  $\text{Li}_{9.54}\text{Si}_{1.74}\text{P}_{1.44}\text{S}_{11.7}\text{Cl}_{0.3}$  (25 mS·cm<sup>-1</sup>)<sup>17</sup> which exhibits the highest room temperature lithium ion conductivity to date.

nodes.title: Theoretical Predictions for Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 System
nodes.text: Recently, Richards et al. 18 used density functional theory and *ab initio* molecular dynamics to investigate the Li<sub>1+2x</sub>Zn<sub>1-x</sub>PS<sub>4</sub> (LZPS) system, which exhibits a bodycentered cubic (bcc) sulfur sublattice. Theory suggests that this arrangement of sulfur atoms, which is also adopted by two other fast ion conductors (Li<sub>7</sub>P<sub>3</sub>S<sub>11</sub> and LGPS), is correlated to a low lithium migration barrier. 19 The stoichiometric parent phase LiZnPS<sub>4</sub> and its optical properties have been previously reported but no ionic conductivity data was provided. 20,21 Its structure consists of a frame-ACS Paragon Plus on the 2d site. work of  $PS_4^{3-}$  and  $ZnS_4^{6-}$  tetrahedra that house Li<sup>+</sup> ions, where Li fully occupies the 2b site and Zn fully occupies the 2a site (**Figure 1a**). In the Li<sub>1+2x</sub>Zn<sub>1-x</sub>PS<sub>4</sub> nonstoichiometric phases (**Figure 1b**) the additional Li shares the 2a site with Zn as we show below, with the excess Li distributing equally between the 2a and an additional site, 2d. This 2d site is close to the "interstitial" site that was not explicitly identified in the theoretical work.<sup>17</sup> The stoichiometric phase was predicted to have extremely poor conductivity based on first-principles calculations (1.81 x  $10^{-12}$  S·cm<sup>-1</sup>, E<sub>a</sub> = 1.07 eV), while the introduction of interstitial lithium defects is predicted to yield ionic conductivities greater than  $5 \times 10^{-2}$  S·cm<sup>-1</sup> (with E<sub>a</sub> > 0.17 eV) at room temperature up to a solid solution solubility limit of x = 0.5; <sup>18</sup> i.e., Li<sub>2.0</sub>Zn<sub>0.5</sub>PS<sub>4</sub>.

nodes.title: Synthesis and Initial Structural Observations
nodes.text: Here, we report the synthesis of the solid solution series, and the structure of the member within the solubility limit with the highest predicted conductivity, derived from combined X-ray and neutron powder diffraction analysis. __IMG_4ac56e04__ **Figure 1.** a) Crystal structure of stoichiometric LiZnPS<sub>4</sub>; b) non-stoichiometric, showing addition of interstitial Li in the 2a site shared between Li and Zn and partial occupancy of Li for the Advistor. The highest value of x (i.e. of lithium excess) in a well crystallized sample was x = 0.35, corresponding to Li1.7Zn0.65PS4. We unequivocally identify lithium occupation of the 2d site, which is charge compensated by substitution of a Zn2+ ion in the 2a site with Li<sup>+</sup> and is crucial for improving ionic transport. Experimental ionic conductivities (σi) measured by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) show that the σiof the most highly conductive phases are in the range of > 10-4 S·cm-1 at 25˚C: a very significant improvement over LiZnPS4, albeit less than predicted. Phases with high values of x (> 0.5) were experimentally unattainable as relatively pure crystalline phases, however. Our observations demonstrate that the enhancement in ionic conductivity observed in the x = 0.75 phase is likely due to a glass-ceramic matrix effect rather than from its inherent crystalline structure. Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 compositions were prepared at x = 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75 using solid-state synthesis consisting of ballmilling and annealing. Their synchrotron x-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns are shown in **Figure 2**. The compositions contain small impurities of Li4P2S6 and ZnS which form upon slight decomposition of the LZPS solid solutions because of their metastable nature. As the lithium content increases (up to x = 0.75), the formation of significant γ-Li3PS4 impurities becomes evident, in accord with the pseudo-binary phase diagram calculated by Richards *et al.*<sup>18</sup> . __IMG_4b3802f7__ **Figure 2. ** Synchrotron powder X-ray diffraction patterns (25°C) of Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 (x = 0.25), Li2Zn0.5PS<sup>4</sup> (x = 0.5), and Li2.5Zn0.75PS4 (x = 0.75) with impurities of Li4P2S6, ZnS, and Li3PS<sup>4</sup> as marked. Region with the dashed box is expanded on the right, indicating the shift in the (112) reflection (4 space group) towards higher angle. The corresponding synthesis temperatures are listed above the compositions. The *a* and *c* lattice parameters were extracted by performing a Pawley full powder pattern fit of the synchrotron XRD patterns in the 4 space group. The trends are shown in **Figure 3** (with exact values given in **Table S1**), indicating that the cell volume increases with increased lithium content (293 Å<sup>3</sup> to 301 Å3). The increase in cell volume stems from a significant increase in the *a* lattice parameter (with a small decrease in the *c* lattice parameter). Larger lattice volume often correlates to an improvement in ionic conductivity due to a reduced Li<sup>+</sup> ion migration barrier. 19, 22

nodes.title: Ionic Conductivity Measurements and Correlation with Structure
nodes.text: Experimental ionic conductivities (σi) measured by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) show that the σiof the most highly conductive phases are in the range of > 10-4 S·cm-1 at 25˚C: a very significant improvement over LiZnPS4, albeit less than predicted. Phases with high values of x (> 0.5) were experimentally unattainable as relatively pure crystalline phases, however. Our observations demonstrate that the enhancement in ionic conductivity observed in the x = 0.75 phase is likely due to a glass-ceramic matrix effect rather than from its inherent crystalline structure. Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 compositions were prepared at x = 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75 using solid-state synthesis consisting of ballmilling and annealing. Their synchrotron x-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns are shown in **Figure 2**. The compositions contain small impurities of Li4P2S6 and ZnS which form upon slight decomposition of the LZPS solid solutions because of their metastable nature. As the lithium content increases (up to x = 0.75), the formation of significant γ-Li3PS4 impurities becomes evident, in accord with the pseudo-binary phase diagram calculated by Richards *et al.*<sup>18</sup> . __IMG_4b3802f7__ **Figure 2. ** Synchrotron powder X-ray diffraction patterns (25°C) of Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 (x = 0.25), Li2Zn0.5PS<sup>4</sup> (x = 0.5), and Li2.5Zn0.75PS4 (x = 0.75) with impurities of Li4P2S6, ZnS, and Li3PS<sup>4</sup> as marked. Region with the dashed box is expanded on the right, indicating the shift in the (112) reflection (4 space group) towards higher angle. The corresponding synthesis temperatures are listed above the compositions. The *a* and *c* lattice parameters were extracted by performing a Pawley full powder pattern fit of the synchrotron XRD patterns in the 4 space group. The trends are shown in **Figure 3** (with exact values given in **Table S1**), indicating that the cell volume increases with increased lithium content (293 Å<sup>3</sup> to 301 Å3). The increase in cell volume stems from a significant increase in the *a* lattice parameter (with a small decrease in the *c* lattice parameter). Larger lattice volume often correlates to an improvement in ionic conductivity due to a reduced Li<sup>+</sup> ion migration barrier. 19, 22 Since the targeted Li2Zn0.5PS4 phase is expected to have the highest ionic conductivity within the solid solution solubility limit, its crystal structure was refined against combined synchrotron powder X-ray diffraction data (λ = 0.412 Å) and time-of-flight (TOF) neutron diffraction data. __IMG_05eac418__ **Figure 3. ** Lattice parameter and volume change in Li1+2xZn1 <sup>x</sup>PS<sup>4</sup> for x = 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75. Solid black circles are from single crystal data taken from the literature<sup>19</sup> and blue squares are experimental data from this work (values are listed in **Table S1**). The reflections were assigned to a body-centered tetragonal cell (space group 4, no. 82) with lattice parameters refined to *a* = 5.7945(2) Å, and *c* = 8.8337(3) Å. The crystallographic details are summarized in **Table 1a** (we note that bond lengths, **Table S2**, are typical for all environments) while the fit for the synchrotron and neutron data is shown in **Figure 4**. The results of the refinement indicate that the actual lithium content of the crystalline material is x ≈ 0.35; lower than that targeted (i.e. x = 0.5). The crystalline __IMG_cadbbb6f__ **Figure 4.** Combined Rietveld refinement of "Li2.0Zn0.5PS4" based on synchrotron x-ray diffraction and neutron diffraction data. Visual representation of the refined crystal structure (refined to a composition of Li1.7Zn0.65PS4) is shown as an inset. Excluded regions correspond to impurity phases, mainly Li4P2S6 which comprises < 5% of the total (see **Figure 2**). **Table 1a. ** Atomic coordinates, Wyckoff symbols, and isotropic displacement parameters for the targeted Li2Zn0.5PS4 phase in the space group 4 (no. 82). the space group 14 (no. 82). __TBL_1c36e98c__ Li1.687Zn0.656PS4 (i.e., Li1.7Zn0.65PS4) phase thus exists in an amorphous Li-rich thiophosphate matrix. The degree of crystallinity was estimated to be 69% using Si as an internal reference (**Figure S1**). A proposed mixture of [77% Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 + 23% *a*-Li3PS4] accounts for the overall "Li2.0Zn0.5PS4" target. The 8% discrepancy may be attributed to the impurity phases (Fig. 2). The refined structure of Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 shows that the 2a sites are partially occupied by Li (34%) and Zn (66%) while the 2d site has partial occupancy of Li (34%) as visually represented in the inset in **Figure 4**. Owing to the well-known difficulty in simultaneously refining thermal parameters and occupancies, the thermal parameters for the 2d and 2b site were fixed to average values from the literature.11,17,23,24 This resulted in convergence to site occupancies that yielded perfect charge balance of the compound and an equal distribution of excess Li on the 2d and 2a sites as expected. The results are in excellent accord with *ab initio* molecular dynamics studies that predict significant lithium ion density on an "interstitial site",17 which is similar to the 2d Wyckoff site we identify. While Li2.5Zn0.25PS4 (x = 0.75) was projected by theory to have the highest conductivity (1.14 x 10-1 S·cm-1),17 its structure could not be refined owing to the low quality of the X-ray and neutron data for this poorly crystallized compound. This is in accord with it lying just out of the predicted solubility limit.17 The structure of "Li1.5Zn0.75PS4" was refined from the synchrotron X-ray data owing to its low lithium content (and a paucity of neutron time); and these results are shown in **Table 1b. ** The fit is shown in **Figure 5;** refined bond lengths (**Table S2**) correspond to typical values for all environments. The lattice __IMG_45dfd1e6__ **Figure 5. ** Rietveld refinement of "Li1.5Zn0.75PS4" synchrotron x-ray diffraction data only. Excluded regions correspond to impurity phases, mainly Li4P2S6, which comprises <10% of the total (see **Figure 2**). **Table 1b. ** Atomic coordinates, Wyckoff symbols, and isotropic displacement parameters for the targeted Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 phase in the space group 4 (no. 82) __TBL_bfa96bd2__ parameters refined to *a* = 5.7641(1) Å, and *c* = 8.8438(2) Å. Since lithium can not be accurately refined from X-ray data, lithium occupation in the 2d and 2a site was fixed to be equal, as determined by the Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 formulation. The Zn occupancy was refined and the vacant occupancy was assumed to be lithium given that the 2a site occupancy is constrained to 1*.* The refined composition of Li1.2Zn0.9PS<sup>4</sup> (with a 70% degree of crystallinity determined by standard addition) shows that the target composition was also not achieved in this case. This may be due to slow kinetics of the reaction that prevent achievement of the targeted lithium contents, despite the employment of nano-sized ZnS in the synthesis (see Supporting Information). However, synthesis at higher temperature or longer times is limited by thermodynamics: due to the metastability of the substoichiometric phases, the LZPS structure partially decomposes to Li4P2S6. The formation of such impurity phases can be prevented by heating at lower temperatures; however, this comes at the cost of reduced degree of crystallinity. The importance of excess phonon free energy in stabilizing defect-type ionic conductors with highly mobile Li<sup>+</sup> ion lattices has been previously invoked, for example, in Li7P3S11, and especially in Li1+2xZn1-xPS4.17 We note that the limiting composition Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 (x = 0.35) is approximately halfway between the predicted solubility limit for the solid solution series without phonon contributions (x = 0.15) and with phonon contributions (x = 0.5)18. Clearly Li1.2Zn0.9PS4 (x = 0.1) falls within in the regime where phonon contributions are not necessary to stabilize the material. All experimental attempts to increase the degree of lithium substitution to attain x = 0.5 were unsuccessful irrespective of temperature, time and processing conditions - and resulted in significant levels of impurity phases. These results confirm that phonon contributions do play a vital role in stabilizing these defect structures but likely to a lower degree than presumed. Partial occupancy of Li in the 2a and 2d site in the LZPS structure should facilitate the ion conduction by creating low energy percolating pathways through the structure. The Li<sup>+</sup> ion conductivity of the various LZPS compositions was studied using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) on pressed pellets at variable temperatures. The impedance spectra in Nyquist form showed classic semicircles at high frequency, and a linear Warburg component in the low-frequency range (**Figure 6a)**. Fitting the data (see inset for equivalent circuit and **Table S3** for fit parameters) resulted in experimental conductivities at 25°C plotted in **Figure 6b** as a function of lithium content. __IMG_0f13aceb__ **Figure 6.* * a) Activation energy plot of Li2Zn0.5PS<sup>4</sup> and Li1.5Zn0.75PS<sup>4</sup> along with an inset of the Nyquist plots at each temperature plus the equivalent circuit used to fit the impedance data and b) Li<sup>+</sup> ion conductivity at 25˚C versus x in Li1+2xZn1-xPS4**. ** Predicted values are taken from ref. 18. The conductivities range from 5.40 × 10-8 S·cm-1 at x = 0 to 8.4 × 10-4 S·cm-1 at x = 0.75. The conductivity of the refined phase Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 was 1.30×10-4 S·cm-1, which is lower than predicted for either Li2.0Zn0.5PS4 (5.38 x 10-2 S·cm-1) or Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 (2.77 x 10-2 S·cm-1) as shown in **Figure 6**. The amorphous content may be responsible, although temperature-dependent conductivity measurements exhibit Arrhenius behavior with a low activation energy of 0.22 eV. This value is close to the range predicted by MD simulations for the defect phases,18 namely 0.165 eV (Li2.0Zn0.5PS4) and 0.181 eV (Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 ). While the possible amorphous phase (i.e., *a*-Li3PS4; σi = 2.8×10-4 S·cm-1 ) <sup>25</sup> may contribute to the overall conductivity, its much lower reported activation energy of 0.4 eV suggests that the σi of Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 dominates. Similarly, the refined phase Li1.2Zn0.9PS4 has a room temperature ionic conductivity of 1.65×10-5 S·cm-1, which is lower than the predicted Li1.25Zn0.875PS4 phase (3.44×10-3 S·cm-1), but the activation energy is 0.25 eV, quite close to theory (0.252 eV18).

nodes.title: Role of Glass-Ceramic Matrix in High Ionic Conductivity
nodes.text: Phases with high values of x (> 0.5) were experimentally unattainable as relatively pure crystalline phases, however. Our observations demonstrate that the enhancement in ionic conductivity observed in the x = 0.75 phase is likely due to a glass-ceramic matrix effect rather than from its inherent crystalline structure. Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 compositions were prepared at x = 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75 using solid-state synthesis consisting of ballmilling and annealing. Their synchrotron x-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns are shown in **Figure 2**. The compositions contain small impurities of Li4P2S6 and ZnS which form upon slight decomposition of the LZPS solid solutions because of their metastable nature. As the lithium content increases (up to x = 0.75), the formation of significant γ-Li3PS4 impurities becomes evident, in accord with the pseudo-binary phase diagram calculated by Richards *et al.*<sup>18</sup> . __IMG_4b3802f7__ **Figure 2. ** Synchrotron powder X-ray diffraction patterns (25°C) of Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 (x = 0.25), Li2Zn0.5PS<sup>4</sup> (x = 0.5), and Li2.5Zn0.75PS4 (x = 0.75) with impurities of Li4P2S6, ZnS, and Li3PS<sup>4</sup> as marked. Region with the dashed box is expanded on the right, indicating the shift in the (112) reflection (4 space group) towards higher angle. The corresponding synthesis temperatures are listed above the compositions. The *a* and *c* lattice parameters were extracted by performing a Pawley full powder pattern fit of the synchrotron XRD patterns in the 4 space group. The trends are shown in **Figure 3** (with exact values given in **Table S1**), indicating that the cell volume increases with increased lithium content (293 Å<sup>3</sup> to 301 Å3). The increase in cell volume stems from a significant increase in the *a* lattice parameter (with a small decrease in the *c* lattice parameter). Larger lattice volume often correlates to an improvement in ionic conductivity due to a reduced Li<sup>+</sup> ion migration barrier. 19, 22 Since the targeted Li2Zn0.5PS4 phase is expected to have the highest ionic conductivity within the solid solution solubility limit, its crystal structure was refined against combined synchrotron powder X-ray diffraction data (λ = 0.412 Å) and time-of-flight (TOF) neutron diffraction data. __IMG_05eac418__ **Figure 3. ** Lattice parameter and volume change in Li1+2xZn1 <sup>x</sup>PS<sup>4</sup> for x = 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75. Solid black circles are from single crystal data taken from the literature<sup>19</sup> and blue squares are experimental data from this work (values are listed in **Table S1**). The reflections were assigned to a body-centered tetragonal cell (space group 4, no. 82) with lattice parameters refined to *a* = 5.7945(2) Å, and *c* = 8.8337(3) Å. The crystallographic details are summarized in **Table 1a** (we note that bond lengths, **Table S2**, are typical for all environments) while the fit for the synchrotron and neutron data is shown in **Figure 4**. The results of the refinement indicate that the actual lithium content of the crystalline material is x ≈ 0.35; lower than that targeted (i.e. x = 0.5). The crystalline __IMG_cadbbb6f__ **Figure 4.** Combined Rietveld refinement of "Li2.0Zn0.5PS4" based on synchrotron x-ray diffraction and neutron diffraction data. Visual representation of the refined crystal structure (refined to a composition of Li1.7Zn0.65PS4) is shown as an inset. Excluded regions correspond to impurity phases, mainly Li4P2S6 which comprises < 5% of the total (see **Figure 2**). **Table 1a. ** Atomic coordinates, Wyckoff symbols, and isotropic displacement parameters for the targeted Li2Zn0.5PS4 phase in the space group 4 (no. 82). the space group 14 (no. 82). __TBL_1c36e98c__ Li1.687Zn0.656PS4 (i.e., Li1.7Zn0.65PS4) phase thus exists in an amorphous Li-rich thiophosphate matrix. The degree of crystallinity was estimated to be 69% using Si as an internal reference (**Figure S1**). A proposed mixture of [77% Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 + 23% *a*-Li3PS4] accounts for the overall "Li2.0Zn0.5PS4" target. The 8% discrepancy may be attributed to the impurity phases (Fig. 2). The refined structure of Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 shows that the 2a sites are partially occupied by Li (34%) and Zn (66%) while the 2d site has partial occupancy of Li (34%) as visually represented in the inset in **Figure 4**. Owing to the well-known difficulty in simultaneously refining thermal parameters and occupancies, the thermal parameters for the 2d and 2b site were fixed to average values from the literature.11,17,23,24 This resulted in convergence to site occupancies that yielded perfect charge balance of the compound and an equal distribution of excess Li on the 2d and 2a sites as expected. The results are in excellent accord with *ab initio* molecular dynamics studies that predict significant lithium ion density on an "interstitial site",17 which is similar to the 2d Wyckoff site we identify. While Li2.5Zn0.25PS4 (x = 0.75) was projected by theory to have the highest conductivity (1.14 x 10-1 S·cm-1),17 its structure could not be refined owing to the low quality of the X-ray and neutron data for this poorly crystallized compound. This is in accord with it lying just out of the predicted solubility limit.17 The structure of "Li1.5Zn0.75PS4" was refined from the synchrotron X-ray data owing to its low lithium content (and a paucity of neutron time); and these results are shown in **Table 1b. ** The fit is shown in **Figure 5;** refined bond lengths (**Table S2**) correspond to typical values for all environments. The lattice __IMG_45dfd1e6__ **Figure 5. ** Rietveld refinement of "Li1.5Zn0.75PS4" synchrotron x-ray diffraction data only. Excluded regions correspond to impurity phases, mainly Li4P2S6, which comprises <10% of the total (see **Figure 2**). **Table 1b. ** Atomic coordinates, Wyckoff symbols, and isotropic displacement parameters for the targeted Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 phase in the space group 4 (no. 82) __TBL_bfa96bd2__ parameters refined to *a* = 5.7641(1) Å, and *c* = 8.8438(2) Å. Since lithium can not be accurately refined from X-ray data, lithium occupation in the 2d and 2a site was fixed to be equal, as determined by the Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 formulation. The Zn occupancy was refined and the vacant occupancy was assumed to be lithium given that the 2a site occupancy is constrained to 1*.* The refined composition of Li1.2Zn0.9PS<sup>4</sup> (with a 70% degree of crystallinity determined by standard addition) shows that the target composition was also not achieved in this case. This may be due to slow kinetics of the reaction that prevent achievement of the targeted lithium contents, despite the employment of nano-sized ZnS in the synthesis (see Supporting Information). However, synthesis at higher temperature or longer times is limited by thermodynamics: due to the metastability of the substoichiometric phases, the LZPS structure partially decomposes to Li4P2S6. The formation of such impurity phases can be prevented by heating at lower temperatures; however, this comes at the cost of reduced degree of crystallinity. The importance of excess phonon free energy in stabilizing defect-type ionic conductors with highly mobile Li<sup>+</sup> ion lattices has been previously invoked, for example, in Li7P3S11, and especially in Li1+2xZn1-xPS4.17 We note that the limiting composition Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 (x = 0.35) is approximately halfway between the predicted solubility limit for the solid solution series without phonon contributions (x = 0.15) and with phonon contributions (x = 0.5)18. Clearly Li1.2Zn0.9PS4 (x = 0.1) falls within in the regime where phonon contributions are not necessary to stabilize the material. All experimental attempts to increase the degree of lithium substitution to attain x = 0.5 were unsuccessful irrespective of temperature, time and processing conditions - and resulted in significant levels of impurity phases. These results confirm that phonon contributions do play a vital role in stabilizing these defect structures but likely to a lower degree than presumed. Partial occupancy of Li in the 2a and 2d site in the LZPS structure should facilitate the ion conduction by creating low energy percolating pathways through the structure. The Li<sup>+</sup> ion conductivity of the various LZPS compositions was studied using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) on pressed pellets at variable temperatures. The impedance spectra in Nyquist form showed classic semicircles at high frequency, and a linear Warburg component in the low-frequency range (**Figure 6a)**. Fitting the data (see inset for equivalent circuit and **Table S3** for fit parameters) resulted in experimental conductivities at 25°C plotted in **Figure 6b** as a function of lithium content. __IMG_0f13aceb__ **Figure 6.* * a) Activation energy plot of Li2Zn0.5PS<sup>4</sup> and Li1.5Zn0.75PS<sup>4</sup> along with an inset of the Nyquist plots at each temperature plus the equivalent circuit used to fit the impedance data and b) Li<sup>+</sup> ion conductivity at 25˚C versus x in Li1+2xZn1-xPS4**. ** Predicted values are taken from ref. 18. The conductivities range from 5.40 × 10-8 S·cm-1 at x = 0 to 8.4 × 10-4 S·cm-1 at x = 0.75. The conductivity of the refined phase Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 was 1.30×10-4 S·cm-1, which is lower than predicted for either Li2.0Zn0.5PS4 (5.38 x 10-2 S·cm-1) or Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 (2.77 x 10-2 S·cm-1) as shown in **Figure 6**. The amorphous content may be responsible, although temperature-dependent conductivity measurements exhibit Arrhenius behavior with a low activation energy of 0.22 eV. This value is close to the range predicted by MD simulations for the defect phases,18 namely 0.165 eV (Li2.0Zn0.5PS4) and 0.181 eV (Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 ). While the possible amorphous phase (i.e., *a*-Li3PS4; σi = 2.8×10-4 S·cm-1 ) <sup>25</sup> may contribute to the overall conductivity, its much lower reported activation energy of 0.4 eV suggests that the σi of Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 dominates. Similarly, the refined phase Li1.2Zn0.9PS4 has a room temperature ionic conductivity of 1.65×10-5 S·cm-1, which is lower than the predicted Li1.25Zn0.875PS4 phase (3.44×10-3 S·cm-1), but the activation energy is 0.25 eV, quite close to theory (0.252 eV18). The highest ionic conductivity of 8.4 x 10-4 S·cm-1 was achieved when the x = 0.75 glassy precursor was heated at lower temperatures (230˚C) to form a very poorly crystallized material. An SEM image of its featureless morphology is shown in **Figure S2**. Heating above that temperature results in a lower ionic conductivity of 2.4 x 10-4 S·cm-1 , and clear phase separation of the LZPS solid solution and γ-Li3PS4. The high conductivity in the glassy phase formed at low temperature is exclusive to the x = 0.75 compound (**Table S3**). Postulating that the improvement in ionic conductivity arises from the glass-ceramic nature of the material, we probed the local structure of Li2.5Zn0.25PS4 via Raman spectroscopy, and compared it to the other two phases. (**Figure S3**). While Li2.0Zn0.5PS4 and Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 show predominantly PS<sup>4</sup> 3- moieties characteristic of the crystalline structure (along with Li4P2S6 impurity), the more highly conductive Li2.5Zn0.25PS4 synthesized at low-temperature contains an additional peak in the Raman spectrum not present in the other two compositions. It corresponds to P2S<sup>7</sup> 4- units; inherent building blocks in the crystalline fast lithium ion conductor Li7P3S11. 16 They exist in its amorphous precursor (70:30 Li2S-P2S5 glass), which is known to have very high conductivities of >10-4 S·cm-1 before annealing 25. This leads us to propose that the glassy matrix plays a significant role in the high ionic conductivity of "Li2.5Zn0.25PS4", rather than inherently enhanced pathways in the structure. In summary, our results provide an understanding of ion transport in the Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 solid solution series by defining the complex relationship between lithium site occupation/position and ionic conductivity. *Ab initio* computational techniques provide inspiration and guidance in the search for new solid-state ion conductors. Here, we have compared the results of introducing interstitial lithium defects in in the solid solution regime Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 predicted by theory, with that of experiment. The stability of the defect phases owing to phonon contributions may be somewhat overestimated by theory, as all phases are found to be highly metastable. Such metastability results in difficulty in overcoming the kinetics necessary for mass transport in order to access the pure phases at the low temperatures required for their synthesis. Nonetheless, phases close to the targeted Li2.0Zn0.5PS4 and Li1.5Zn0.75PS<sup>4</sup> were successfully synthesized. Their structures were elucidated via refinement of diffraction data. The obtained phases, Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 and Li1.2Zn0.9PS4 respectively, demonstrated ionic conductivities of 1.30×10-4 S·cm-1 and 1.65×10-5 S·cm-1. These values are more than four orders of magnitude higher compared to that of the parent LiZnPS4 phase, owing to occupation of the 2d interstitial site in the lattice as predicted by theory. This represents a good demonstration of how information from *ab initio* molecular dynamics can augment experiment, similar to Li10GeP2S12, where early reports using powder diffraction alone could not locate a lithium site important to 3D mobility, but a combination of theory and single crystal diffraction enabled full structure resolution.11,26–28 While our experimental lithium ion conductivities were lower than predicted, this can be ascribed to a combination of not fully accessing the targeted lithium defect concentrations (owing to the limitations of kinetics and thermodynamics), and the accompanying reality of the presence of amorphous and potentially poorly conductive materials. The fact that we can synthesize solid solutions close to the predicted superionic phases is encouraging, however, and suggests that alternate highly non-equilibrium synthetic routes may be required to access pure phases. This should provide further inspiration for future endeavors. Moreover, LZPS compositions at high lithium contents – Li2.5Zn0.25PS4 - exhibit conductivities up to 8 x 10-4 S·cm-1, showing that a glassy matrix can play a key role in governing fast lithium ion conduction.

nodes.title: This value is close to the range predict...
nodes.text: This value is close to the range predicted by MD simulations for the defect phases,18 namely 0.165 eV (Li2.0Zn0.5PS4) and 0.181 eV (Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 ).

nodes.title: While the possible amorphous phase (i.e....
nodes.text: While the possible amorphous phase (i.e., *a*-Li3PS4; σi = 2.8×10-4 S·cm-1 ) <sup>25</sup> may contribute to the overall conductivity, its much lower reported activation energy of 0.4 eV suggests that the σi of Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 dominates.

nodes.title: Similarly, the refined phase Li1.2Zn0.9P...
nodes.text: Similarly, the refined phase Li1.2Zn0.9PS4 has a room temperature ionic conductivity of 1.65×10-5 S·cm-1, which is lower than the predicted Li1.25Zn0.875PS4 phase (3.44×10-3 S·cm-1), but the activation energy is 0.25 eV, quite close to theory (0.252 eV18).

nodes.title: The highest ionic conductivity of 8.4 x ...

nodes.title: Heating above that temperature results i...
nodes.text: Heating above that temperature results in a lower ionic conductivity of 2.4 x 10-4 S·cm-1 , and clear phase separation of the LZPS solid solution and γ-Li3PS4.

nodes.title: The high conductivity in the glassy phas...
nodes.text: The high conductivity in the glassy phase formed at low temperature is exclusive to the x = 0.75 compound (**Table S3**).

nodes.title: Postulating that the improvement in ioni...

nodes.text: They exist in its amorphous precursor (70:30 Li2S-P2S5 glass), which is known to have very high conductivities of >10-4 S·cm-1 before annealing 25.

nodes.title: This leads us to propose that the glassy...
nodes.text: This leads us to propose that the glassy matrix plays a significant role in the high ionic conductivity of "Li2.5Zn0.25PS4", rather than inherently enhanced pathways in the structure.

nodes.title: In summary, our results provide an under...
nodes.text: In summary, our results provide an understanding of ion transport in the Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 solid solution series by defining the complex relationship between lithium site occupation/position and ionic conductivity.

nodes.title: *Ab initio* computational techniques pro...
nodes.text: *Ab initio* computational techniques provide inspiration and guidance in the search for new solid-state ion conductors.

nodes.title: Here, we have compared the results of in...
nodes.text: Here, we have compared the results of introducing interstitial lithium defects in in the solid solution regime Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 predicted by theory, with that of experiment.

nodes.title: The stability of the defect phases owing...
nodes.text: The stability of the defect phases owing to phonon contributions may be somewhat overestimated by theory, as all phases are found to be highly metastable.

nodes.title: Such metastability results in difficulty...
nodes.text: Such metastability results in difficulty in overcoming the kinetics necessary for mass transport in order to access the pure phases at the low temperatures required for their synthesis.

nodes.title: Nonetheless, phases close to the targete...
nodes.text: Nonetheless, phases close to the targeted Li2.0Zn0.5PS4 and Li1.5Zn0.75PS<sup>4</sup> were successfully synthesized.

nodes.title: Their structures were elucidated via ref...
nodes.text: Their structures were elucidated via refinement of diffraction data.

nodes.title: The obtained phases, Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 and ...
nodes.text: The obtained phases, Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 and Li1.2Zn0.9PS4 respectively, demonstrated ionic conductivities of 1.30×10-4 S·cm-1 and 1.65×10-5 S·cm-1.

nodes.title: These values are more than four orders o...
nodes.text: These values are more than four orders of magnitude higher compared to that of the parent LiZnPS4 phase, owing to occupation of the 2d interstitial site in the lattice as predicted by theory.

nodes.title: This represents a good demonstration of ...
nodes.text: This represents a good demonstration of how information from *ab initio* molecular dynamics can augment experiment, similar to Li10GeP2S12, where early reports using powder diffraction alone could not locate a lithium site important to 3D mobility, but a combination of theory and single crystal diffraction enabled full structure resolution.11,26–28 While our experimental lithium ion conductivities were lower than predicted, this can be ascribed to a combination of not fully accessing the targeted lithium defect concentrations (owing to the limitations of kinetics and thermodynamics), and the accompanying reality of the presence of amorphous and potentially poorly conductive materials.

nodes.title: The fact that we can synthesize solid so...
nodes.text: The fact that we can synthesize solid solutions close to the predicted superionic phases is encouraging, however, and suggests that alternate highly non-equilibrium synthetic routes may be required to access pure phases.

nodes.title: This should provide further inspiration ...
nodes.text: This should provide further inspiration for future endeavors.

nodes.title: Moreover, LZPS compositions at high lith...
nodes.text: Moreover, LZPS compositions at high lithium contents – Li2.5Zn0.25PS4 - exhibit conductivities up to 8 x 10-4 S·cm-1, showing that a glassy matrix can play a key role in governing fast lithium ion conduction.

nodes.title: Detailed Structural Refinement of Crystalline Li1+2xZn1-xPS4
nodes.text: Since the targeted Li2Zn0.5PS4 phase is expected to have the highest ionic conductivity within the solid solution solubility limit, its crystal structure was refined against combined synchrotron powder X-ray diffraction data (λ = 0.412 Å) and time-of-flight (TOF) neutron diffraction data. __IMG_05eac418__ **Figure 3. ** Lattice parameter and volume change in Li1+2xZn1 <sup>x</sup>PS<sup>4</sup> for x = 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75. Solid black circles are from single crystal data taken from the literature<sup>19</sup> and blue squares are experimental data from this work (values are listed in **Table S1**). The reflections were assigned to a body-centered tetragonal cell (space group 4, no. 82) with lattice parameters refined to *a* = 5.7945(2) Å, and *c* = 8.8337(3) Å. The crystallographic details are summarized in **Table 1a** (we note that bond lengths, **Table S2**, are typical for all environments) while the fit for the synchrotron and neutron data is shown in **Figure 4**. The results of the refinement indicate that the actual lithium content of the crystalline material is x ≈ 0.35; lower than that targeted (i.e. x = 0.5). The crystalline __IMG_cadbbb6f__ **Figure 4.** Combined Rietveld refinement of "Li2.0Zn0.5PS4" based on synchrotron x-ray diffraction and neutron diffraction data. Visual representation of the refined crystal structure (refined to a composition of Li1.7Zn0.65PS4) is shown as an inset. Excluded regions correspond to impurity phases, mainly Li4P2S6 which comprises < 5% of the total (see **Figure 2**). **Table 1a. ** Atomic coordinates, Wyckoff symbols, and isotropic displacement parameters for the targeted Li2Zn0.5PS4 phase in the space group 4 (no. 82). the space group 14 (no. 82). __TBL_1c36e98c__ Li1.687Zn0.656PS4 (i.e., Li1.7Zn0.65PS4) phase thus exists in an amorphous Li-rich thiophosphate matrix. The degree of crystallinity was estimated to be 69% using Si as an internal reference (**Figure S1**). A proposed mixture of [77% Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 + 23% *a*-Li3PS4] accounts for the overall "Li2.0Zn0.5PS4" target. The 8% discrepancy may be attributed to the impurity phases (Fig. 2). The refined structure of Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 shows that the 2a sites are partially occupied by Li (34%) and Zn (66%) while the 2d site has partial occupancy of Li (34%) as visually represented in the inset in **Figure 4**. Owing to the well-known difficulty in simultaneously refining thermal parameters and occupancies, the thermal parameters for the 2d and 2b site were fixed to average values from the literature.11,17,23,24 This resulted in convergence to site occupancies that yielded perfect charge balance of the compound and an equal distribution of excess Li on the 2d and 2a sites as expected. The results are in excellent accord with *ab initio* molecular dynamics studies that predict significant lithium ion density on an "interstitial site",17 which is similar to the 2d Wyckoff site we identify. While Li2.5Zn0.25PS4 (x = 0.75) was projected by theory to have the highest conductivity (1.14 x 10-1 S·cm-1),17 its structure could not be refined owing to the low quality of the X-ray and neutron data for this poorly crystallized compound. This is in accord with it lying just out of the predicted solubility limit.17 The structure of "Li1.5Zn0.75PS4" was refined from the synchrotron X-ray data owing to its low lithium content (and a paucity of neutron time); and these results are shown in **Table 1b. ** The fit is shown in **Figure 5;** refined bond lengths (**Table S2**) correspond to typical values for all environments. The lattice __IMG_45dfd1e6__ **Figure 5. ** Rietveld refinement of "Li1.5Zn0.75PS4" synchrotron x-ray diffraction data only. Excluded regions correspond to impurity phases, mainly Li4P2S6, which comprises <10% of the total (see **Figure 2**). **Table 1b. ** Atomic coordinates, Wyckoff symbols, and isotropic displacement parameters for the targeted Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 phase in the space group 4 (no. 82) __TBL_bfa96bd2__ parameters refined to *a* = 5.7641(1) Å, and *c* = 8.8438(2) Å. Since lithium can not be accurately refined from X-ray data, lithium occupation in the 2d and 2a site was fixed to be equal, as determined by the Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 formulation. The Zn occupancy was refined and the vacant occupancy was assumed to be lithium given that the 2a site occupancy is constrained to 1*.* The refined composition of Li1.2Zn0.9PS<sup>4</sup> (with a 70% degree of crystallinity determined by standard addition) shows that the target composition was also not achieved in this case.

nodes.title: Experimental Challenges and Discrepancies in Phase Purity
nodes.text: While Li2.5Zn0.25PS4 (x = 0.75) was projected by theory to have the highest conductivity (1.14 x 10-1 S·cm-1),17 its structure could not be refined owing to the low quality of the X-ray and neutron data for this poorly crystallized compound. This is in accord with it lying just out of the predicted solubility limit.17 The structure of "Li1.5Zn0.75PS4" was refined from the synchrotron X-ray data owing to its low lithium content (and a paucity of neutron time); and these results are shown in **Table 1b. ** The fit is shown in **Figure 5;** refined bond lengths (**Table S2**) correspond to typical values for all environments. The lattice __IMG_45dfd1e6__ **Figure 5. ** Rietveld refinement of "Li1.5Zn0.75PS4" synchrotron x-ray diffraction data only. Excluded regions correspond to impurity phases, mainly Li4P2S6, which comprises <10% of the total (see **Figure 2**). **Table 1b. ** Atomic coordinates, Wyckoff symbols, and isotropic displacement parameters for the targeted Li1.5Zn0.75PS4 phase in the space group 4 (no. 82) __TBL_bfa96bd2__ parameters refined to *a* = 5.7641(1) Å, and *c* = 8.8438(2) Å. Since lithium can not be accurately refined from X-ray data, lithium occupation in the 2d and 2a site was fixed to be equal, as determined by the Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 formulation. The Zn occupancy was refined and the vacant occupancy was assumed to be lithium given that the 2a site occupancy is constrained to 1*.* The refined composition of Li1.2Zn0.9PS<sup>4</sup> (with a 70% degree of crystallinity determined by standard addition) shows that the target composition was also not achieved in this case. This may be due to slow kinetics of the reaction that prevent achievement of the targeted lithium contents, despite the employment of nano-sized ZnS in the synthesis (see Supporting Information). However, synthesis at higher temperature or longer times is limited by thermodynamics: due to the metastability of the substoichiometric phases, the LZPS structure partially decomposes to Li4P2S6. The formation of such impurity phases can be prevented by heating at lower temperatures; however, this comes at the cost of reduced degree of crystallinity. The importance of excess phonon free energy in stabilizing defect-type ionic conductors with highly mobile Li<sup>+</sup> ion lattices has been previously invoked, for example, in Li7P3S11, and especially in Li1+2xZn1-xPS4.17 We note that the limiting composition Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 (x = 0.35) is approximately halfway between the predicted solubility limit for the solid solution series without phonon contributions (x = 0.15) and with phonon contributions (x = 0.5)18. Clearly Li1.2Zn0.9PS4 (x = 0.1) falls within in the regime where phonon contributions are not necessary to stabilize the material. All experimental attempts to increase the degree of lithium substitution to attain x = 0.5 were unsuccessful irrespective of temperature, time and processing conditions - and resulted in significant levels of impurity phases. These results confirm that phonon contributions do play a vital role in stabilizing these defect structures but likely to a lower degree than presumed.

nodes.title: Conclusion and Future Outlook
nodes.text: In summary, our results provide an understanding of ion transport in the Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 solid solution series by defining the complex relationship between lithium site occupation/position and ionic conductivity. *Ab initio* computational techniques provide inspiration and guidance in the search for new solid-state ion conductors. Here, we have compared the results of introducing interstitial lithium defects in in the solid solution regime Li1+2xZn1-xPS4 predicted by theory, with that of experiment. The stability of the defect phases owing to phonon contributions may be somewhat overestimated by theory, as all phases are found to be highly metastable. Such metastability results in difficulty in overcoming the kinetics necessary for mass transport in order to access the pure phases at the low temperatures required for their synthesis. Nonetheless, phases close to the targeted Li2.0Zn0.5PS4 and Li1.5Zn0.75PS<sup>4</sup> were successfully synthesized. Their structures were elucidated via refinement of diffraction data. The obtained phases, Li1.7Zn0.65PS4 and Li1.2Zn0.9PS4 respectively, demonstrated ionic conductivities of 1.30×10-4 S·cm-1 and 1.65×10-5 S·cm-1. These values are more than four orders of magnitude higher compared to that of the parent LiZnPS4 phase, owing to occupation of the 2d interstitial site in the lattice as predicted by theory. This represents a good demonstration of how information from *ab initio* molecular dynamics can augment experiment, similar to Li10GeP2S12, where early reports using powder diffraction alone could not locate a lithium site important to 3D mobility, but a combination of theory and single crystal diffraction enabled full structure resolution.11,26–28 While our experimental lithium ion conductivities were lower than predicted, this can be ascribed to a combination of not fully accessing the targeted lithium defect concentrations (owing to the limitations of kinetics and thermodynamics), and the accompanying reality of the presence of amorphous and potentially poorly conductive materials. The fact that we can synthesize solid solutions close to the predicted superionic phases is encouraging, however, and suggests that alternate highly non-equilibrium synthetic routes may be required to access pure phases. This should provide further inspiration for future endeavors.

nodes.text: This represents a good demonstration of how information from *ab initio* molecular dynamics can augment experiment, similar to Li10GeP2S12, where early reports using powder diffraction alone could not locate a lithium site important to 3D mobility, but a combination of theory and single crystal diffraction enabled full structure resolution.11,26–28 While our experimental lithium ion conductivities were lower than predicted, this can be ascribed to a combination of not fully accessing the targeted lithium defect concentrations (owing to the limitations of kinetics and thermodynamics), and the accompanying reality of the presence of amorphous and potentially poorly conductive materials.
